Tailcat client

Source: R/client.R
TailcatClient.Rd

A tailcat client connects to the TailcatServer identified by a secret tailcat address. It can only dial that server. Network startup happens on the first $dial(), $ping(), or $disco_ping().

Blocking methods have an _async() counterpart that returns a promises::promise(); see TailcatServer for how asynchronous results are delivered, for timeouts (including timeout = 0), and for the error classes.

The address is a secret; printing a client never shows it or the private key, and the client does not keep a copy of the address in R.

Once a client is closed, every method other than $close(), $format(), and $print(), and every field other than $is_closed, raises a tailcat_closed error; nothing is kept from before. A client restored from a saved session is closed, because handles do not survive serialization.

A server with an allowlist (allowed_clients or TailcatServer$allow_client()) does not answer clients that are not on it, so for such a client $dial(), $ping(), and $disco_ping() fail with tailcat_timeout once their timeout runs out, rather than with a distinct error.

Active bindings

public_key

The client's public key, for TailcatServer$allow_client(). It is fetched from tailcat on each access.

is_closed

TRUE once the client has been closed.

TailcatClient$new()

Create a client. No network access happens until it is used.

Usage

TailcatClient$new(address, key = NULL, derp_map_url = NULL)

Arguments

address

The server's secret tailcat address (a string or a tailcat_secret). Surrounding whitespace, such as a trailing newline from a file, is ignored.

key

Private node key (a string in text encoding, or a tailcat_keys object from tailcat_keygen()), or NULL to generate one. A stable key gives the client a stable public key, for use with allowed_clients.

derp_map_url

URL of a relay map to use instead of the default, or NULL to use the rtailcat.derp_map_url option (see the section on relay options in TailcatServer) or, when that is unset, the default.

TailcatClient$dial()

Connect to a port on the server.

Usage

TailcatClient$dial(port, network = c("tcp", "udp"), timeout = 30)

Arguments

port

Port number (1 to 65535).

network

Exactly "tcp" (the default) or "udp".

timeout

Seconds to wait, covering relay registration and the connection; Inf waits indefinitely and 0 polls.

Returns

A TailcatConnection.

TailcatClient$dial_async(port, network = c("tcp", "udp"), timeout = 30)

network

Exactly "tcp" (the default) or "udp".

timeout

Seconds to wait; Inf waits indefinitely and 0 polls.

Returns

A promise resolving with a TailcatConnection.

TailcatClient$ping()

Measure the round-trip time to the server through the relay.

Usage

TailcatClient$ping(timeout = 30)

Arguments

timeout

Seconds to wait; Inf waits indefinitely and 0 polls.

Returns

The latency in seconds (a double). tailcat reports whole milliseconds, so the resolution is 0.001 and a ping faster than a millisecond reads as 0. This differs from tailcat's C ABI (tailcat.h), which returns the milliseconds; seconds match $disco_ping() and the timeouts.

TailcatClient$ping_async()

Asynchronous version of $ping().

Usage

TailcatClient$ping_async(timeout = 30)

Arguments

timeout

Seconds to wait; Inf waits indefinitely and 0 polls.

Returns

A promise resolving with the latency in seconds.

TailcatClient$disco_ping()

Send a discovery ping, which also triggers direct path discovery.

Usage

TailcatClient$disco_ping(timeout = 30)

Arguments

timeout

Seconds to wait; use a finite value since discovery may otherwise wait indefinitely.

Returns

A list with latency (seconds), endpoint (the direct path, or "" when relayed), relay_region_id, and relay_region_code (the relay region the ping went through).

TailcatClient$drain()

Wait for TCP shutdown traffic to finish. Call it after closing connections (or reaching end of stream) and before closing the client or exiting R, so the server sees a clean end of stream.

Usage

TailcatClient$drain(timeout = 5)

Arguments

timeout

Seconds to wait. Inf is accepted but waits as long as shutdown takes, which can be indefinitely when a peer has gone away, so a finite value is recommended.

Returns

The client, invisibly.

TailcatClient$drain_async()

Asynchronous version of $drain().

Usage

TailcatClient$drain_async(timeout = 5)

Arguments

timeout

Seconds to wait; as for $drain(), a finite value is recommended.

Returns

A promise resolving with the client.

TailcatClient$close()

Close the client and all of its connections. Closing twice is harmless. Closing tears the client down immediately, so the server may not see the end of its streams until its own reads time out. To give the server a clean end of stream, close the connections first and pass drain, which waits for their shutdown traffic before closing (see $drain()).

Usage

TailcatClient$close(drain = 0)

Arguments

drain

Seconds to wait for TCP shutdown traffic before closing, as for $drain(); 0 (the default) closes at once. A drain that times out or fails does not prevent the close and is not reported.

Returns

The client, invisibly.

TailcatClient$format()

Format a summary, the lines that $print() shows. The address and private key are never shown. A closed client shows only its state.

Usage

TailcatClient$format(...)

Arguments

...

Ignored.

Returns

A character vector.

TailcatClient$print()

Print the summary from $format().

Usage

TailcatClient$print(...)

Arguments

...

Ignored.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
address = readLines("address.txt")
cli = TailcatClient$new(address)
conn = cli$dial(8080)
conn$write("hello\n")
conn$close()
cli$drain()
cli$close()
} # }
